record.paper_title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Causal assumptions for robustness and meta-learning
record.original_question: How can causal assumptions improve adversarial robustness and meta-learning by treating adversarial perturbations or task variables as interventions, and by learning representations that stay invariant across such interventions rather than merely conditioning on observed perturbation or task labels?

evidence.quote: We note two active ML research areas akin to invariance learning: adversarial robustness and meta-learning. We put forward to investigate how causal assumptions may benefit these areas, as it is currently underexplored.

Future work must examine if causal assumptions can be used to learn better task-invariant representations. For example, instead of conditioning on task variables, it could be interesting to explore interventions on them.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a supervised learning setting in which one observes data (X, Y) generated by a structural causal model with latent variables, and in which two types of exogenous perturbations may act on the inputs:

(a) Adversarial perturbations. For each clean input X, an adversary chooses a perturbation δ in a bounded set Δ (e.g., an ℓ_p-ball of radius ε) producing X̃ = X + δ. Model the choice of δ as an intervention do(E = δ) on an exogenous "perturbation" variable E in the structural causal model, rather than as an additional observed covariate to condition on.

(b) Task variables in meta-learning. One observes data from a family of related tasks indexed by a variable T (so that on task t one has a distribution P_t(X, Y)). Model T as an intervention target do(T = t) on shared causal mechanisms, rather than as an observed conditioning variable.

Let Φ: X → Z denote a learned representation, and let f: Z → Y denote a downstream predictor.

Problem. Formulate and analyze conditions on the underlying causal model under which there exist representations Φ that are invariant under the interventional family {do(E = δ) : δ ∈ Δ} (respectively {do(T = t) : t ∈ T}), in the sense that the conditional distribution of Φ(X) given the non-intervened causal parents of Y is the same across all interventions in the family. Specifically:

1. Give sufficient (and, where possible, necessary) structural assumptions on the SCM (e.g., on which mechanisms are shared across interventions, on the support of E or T, and on identifiability of latent causal factors) under which such an invariant representation Φ exists and is identifiable from data drawn under a finite collection of interventions.

2. Prove generalization or robustness guarantees for the predictor f ∘ Φ trained on such invariant representations, comparing:
   (i) the interventional approach (treating E or T as do-interventions and enforcing invariance of Φ across the interventional family), versus
   (ii) the purely conditional approach (treating E or T as observed covariates and conditioning on them),
under distribution shifts in E or T at test time, including shifts to unseen values δ ∉ Δ_train or tasks t ∉ T_train.

3. Provide a learning algorithm that, given samples from several interventional regimes, recovers such an invariant representation, together with finite-sample bounds on its adversarial risk (for case (a)) and on its few-shot meta-learning risk on new tasks (for case (b)).

Determine whether causal-interventional formulations of E and T provably yield strictly better worst-case robustness and task-transfer guarantees than non-causal approaches that merely condition on observed perturbation or task labels.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an underexplored research direction. While there is active work on causal invariance, invariant risk minimization, and causal representation learning relevant to adversarial robustness and meta-learning, no comprehensive resolution providing the structural conditions, identifiability results, and provable robustness/transfer guarantees described above is established. The direction remains open.

status_evidence.title: Causal Machine Learning: A Survey and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Lists adversarial robustness and meta-learning under causal invariance as underexplored open directions.
status_evidence.claim: The connection between causal interventions and adversarial robustness/meta-learning is identified as an open research problem.

status_evidence.title: Invariant Risk Minimization (Arjovsky et al.)
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes invariance across environments but does not resolve identifiability or provide adversarial-robustness guarantees in the interventional sense described.
status_evidence.claim: Related invariance-based approaches exist but do not fully answer the problem.
